rows.name: context-16-frozen-16
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Because a timeout means the client doesn’t know whether the charge succeeded—not that it failed. Reusing the same durable idempotency key lets the server recognize the retry and return the original outcome, while atomic key reservation prevents concurrent requests from charging twice. The charge and its durable outcome must commit atomically; otherwise, a crash between them could leave a completed charge with no record. For an external payment provider, use its idempotency support with the same stable key and reconcile the result, since a local database transaction alone cannot make the external charge atomic.

review.note: Unknown timeout outcome needs stable durable key and atomic ownership/outcome. External provider charge correctly requires provider idempotency/reconciliation; no invented local-transaction guarantee.
review.usefulPrefix: Because a timeout means the client doesn’t know whether the charge succeeded—not that it failed. rows.name: context-30-frozen-30
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it does not prevent concurrent transactions from making decisions using stale snapshots. Initially Alice and Bob are both on call: each transaction reads both rows, checks that the other person remains, and takes its own person off call. Under snapshot isolation, they update different rows, so both can commit and leave nobody on call. No serial execution permits that result: the second transaction would see only one person remaining and refuse to remove them, which is why atomicity alone does not guarantee serializability.
